practical.title: Your First C Program: Hello, World!
practical.sourceActivity: Your First C Program: Hello, World!

coachingPrompts: What do you predict will happen before you run it?
What evidence shows that your change worked?
Can you explain the result in your own words?

teachingPlaylist.title: Observe the Baseline Program
teachingPlaylist.description: Compile and run greeting.c as provided to see the default 'Hello, World!' output.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand how #include, main, printf, and \n produce console output.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: We'll run the starter program as-is. Watch the terminal and match the output to the printf line in the file. Notice the newline escapes and why the prompt appears on the next line.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You inherited a small utility that prints a status message. Verifying it prints correctly helps ensure it's installed properly.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Predict the program's output. Then compile and run and describe whether your prediction was correct.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Not saving the file before compiling — ensure you saved edits before running clang.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You ran the program and linked the printf line to the terminal output.
codeSteps: Open greeting.c and read the file.

teachingPlaylist.title: Edit the Greeting
teachingPlaylist.description: Modify the printf string to a personalized message and re-run the program.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Practice the edit → compile → run workflow and see immediate feedback from a one-line change.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Change the string literal inside printf to your name or a short message. Recompile and run to see how the terminal output changes.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Change to printf("Hello, Cohortia Learner!\n"); then clang greeting.c -o greeting && ./greeting
teachingPlaylist.scenario: Customizing a program's startup message for a specific user or environment.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Edit the string, recompile, and confirm the new message appears exactly as you typed it.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Forgetting to keep the double quotes around the string or forgetting the closing parenthesis and semicolon.
teachingPlaylist.recap: A single-line text change updates what the program prints when run.
codeSteps: Edit greeting.c: change the printf string.
Run: ./greeting and verify the personalized text.

teachingPlaylist.title: Experiment with Newlines and Multiple printf Calls
teachingPlaylist.description: Try removing the trailing newline and add another printf to observe concatenated output.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Understand how escape sequences and multiple print calls affect terminal output layout.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Remove the \n from the first printf and add a second printf that ends with \n. Compile and observe that the two messages appear on one line.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: First printf without \n followed by a second printf with \n: outputs combined message on a single line.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: Constructing status lines where parts of a message are produced by different functions.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Make the change and predict whether output will be on one or two lines, then test your prediction.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Assuming each printf automatically adds a newline — it only does if you include \n.
teachingPlaylist.recap: Newlines control cursor movement; multiple printf calls concatenate if no newline intervenes.
codeSteps: Edit greeting.c: remove \n from the first printf and add a second printf ending with \n.

teachingPlaylist.title: Make an Error, Read the Compiler, and Fix It
teachingPlaylist.description: Intentionally remove a semicolon to see the compiler error, then fix it and extend the greeting.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Learn how to read compiler diagnostics and confidently fix syntax errors.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Remove the semicolon after return 0 and compile. Read the error message; it points to the syntax problem. Restore the semicolon and change the greeting to a new scenario like 'Good morning'.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Remove semicolon → clang prints an error mentioning 'expected' or 'error' → restore semicolon → recompile successfully.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: Fixing a broken build in a codebase by reading compiler output.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: When you see the compiler error, note the line number and message. Explain in your own words what the message is telling you.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Panicking at compiler output; instead, read it—errors usually indicate the file and approximate location.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You caused and fixed a syntax error and extended the program with a new greeting.
codeSteps: Edit greeting.c: remove semicolon after return 0 and save.
Run: clang greeting.c -o greeting (observe the error)
Fix the file: add the semicolon back and change the message.
Run: clang greeting.c -o greeting && ./greeting to confirm 'Good morning...' prints.

tasks.title: Scene 1 — Observe & Understand
tasks.narratorGuide: Let's run the provided greeting.c exactly as-is. We'll compile with clang and then execute the produced program. As you watch the output, connect it to the printf line in the source file. Notice the \n at the end of the string — that moves the cursor to the next line after printing. Predict what will appear in the terminal before running. Pause after you run it, then explain in one sentence what each marked line does.

tasks.title: Scene 2 — Modify & Experiment
tasks.narratorGuide: Edit the printf line so it prints your name or a custom message, for example "Hello, Cohortia Learner!\n". Save the file, recompile with clang, and run the executable. Predict what changes in the terminal output and confirm. This small change demonstrates the edit-compile-run feedback loop that is central to C development.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — Build & Integrate
tasks.narratorGuide: First, remove the trailing \n from the first printf and add a second printf that finishes the sentence and includes \n. Compile and run to observe that the two printf calls produce contiguous output when the first lacks a newline. Predict the exact printed line before running. This shows how output is buffered and how newlines affect terminal layout.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — Verify & Extend
tasks.narratorGuide: First, deliberately remove the semicolon from the return statement and try compiling to observe the compiler error. Read the error message: it points to a syntax issue. Then restore the semicolon and compile successfully. Finally, change the greeting to a new real-world message such as 'Good morning, <your name>!' and verify the output. Compiler errors are teaching moments—read them carefully.
